studies.label: 24-week classroom intervention: ChatGPT-4-supported vs traditional music instruction
studies.cluster_se_treatment: Class-level random assignment is explicitly reported (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1), but class counts and the allocation procedure are not given. Neither the MANCOVA nor the latent growth model reports standard errors clustered by class or class-level random effects (PDF pp. 8-9, Sections 3.7 and 4; Tables 3, 5, and 6). Growth-model random intercept and slope factors describe students, not randomized classes. Reported precision does not establish valid class-level uncertainty.

arms.name: Experimental (ChatGPT-4 supported)
arms.description: Students used ChatGPT-4 throughout music coursework for melodic, harmonic, and structural suggestions, compositional feedback, improvisation prompts, analytical checks, and arranging support. They were encouraged to evaluate, adapt, and integrate its output and submitted screenshots or links of their interactions. Same instructor as control (PDF pp. 5-7, Sections 3.2 and 3.6 and Table 1).

arms.name: Control (traditional instruction)
arms.description: Equivalent music tasks with traditional teacher-led instruction, textbooks, class notes, lectures, handouts, and teacher feedback, without AI augmentation. Same instructor as the experimental group (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 3.2 and Table 1).

studies.task: Second-year Bachelor of Music students produced compositions, recorded improvisations, reharmonizations, stylistic adaptations, and arrangements, with accompanying analytical tasks, during normal coursework.

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT-4 (identified as ChatGPT-4o in Section 3.1)
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 3.1 (the newer generation of ChatGPT-4, i.e., ChatGPT-4o); PDF p. 4, Section 2.3 (OpenAI, 2024 system announcement); PDF p. 18, References (OpenAI. (2024). GPT-4o system card.)

preregistration.where: No preregistration or trial-registration statement is present in the article; the methodology reports institutional ethics approval only.

studies.shared_sample: Drawn from the cohort in Zhou and Kim (2024), Innovative music education: An empirical assessment of ChatGPT-4’s impact on student learning experiences, Education and Information Technologies, DOI 10.1007/s10639-024-12705-z. This article reports new follow-up coursework data, not a reanalysis of the earlier outcomes. Earlier AI-condition students had structured ChatGPT exposure; whether current allocation retained earlier conditions is not stated. PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; PDF p. 19, References.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Creative products were scored by two external experts in music theory, composition, and creativity research, blinded to student identity, condition, and submission timing. The creativity rubric has four dimensions, each on a seven-point scale: originality of musical ideas, overall musical value, inventiveness in development, and expressive impact. The rubric draws on Webster and the Consensual Assessment Technique. Dimension/rater aggregation and output-score inter-rater reliability are not specified. PDF p. 6, Section 3.3; PDF p. 7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5.

estimates.notes: Univariate group test following MANCOVA, adjusted for prior ChatGPT use, Week 1 creativity, and Week 1 analytical skills (PDF p. 9, Results RQ2). Table 6 explicitly reports adjusted means and standard errors, not SDs. No mean difference, difference SE, confidence interval, or participant-level arm SD is printed. The paper does not specify the measurement occasion or aggregation used as the dependent variable; this is not labeled as a final-session score. The authors call the Week 1 covariates baseline scores, and Section 3.1 says baseline tasks preceded intervention, so this is retained as a reported baseline-adjusted contrast. Whether those Week 1 scores preceded ChatGPT access is unresolved because Table 1 places supported composition in the opening weeks. se_basis=participant describes the paper's student-level analysis, not valid adjustment for the randomized classes; no class-clustered uncertainty is reported. The study total is printed in the abstract, and the analyzed arm counts are printed in Table 6. AI remained available during the assessed coursework; immediate denotes performance during the intervention, not performance after AI withdrawal.

estimates.notes: The mean fields hold arm-specific estimated means of the latent linear slope factor, not observed creativity-score levels or a coefficient for treatment assignment. The paper contrasts the growth rates in Results RQ1 (PDF p. 8), but prints no between-arm slope difference, difference SE, confidence interval, or group test. Table 3 prints the bound < .000 for each arm parameter. These within-arm tests against zero are retained verbatim in the source quote and are not entered as a contrast p-value or silently corrected. The source quote preserves the table's three-decimal precision. The text rounds the same estimates; those are not separate estimates. The latent growth analysis has person-level random intercept and slope factors, with no reported class effects or class-adjusted SEs. se_basis=participant describes that analysis rather than class-level precision. Analysis-specific person counts are not printed for the growth model, so this estimate's n fields are null; study enrollment and Table 6 analyzed counts are recorded separately. The relationship between the growth time step and calendar weeks is unclear: the procedure describes twelve biweekly assessments across twenty-four weeks, while the growth figure labels occasions as weeks. Figure 1 on PDF p. 10 plots the fitted trajectories without numeric labels on the points; no occasion means or endpoints have been read off the graph. Initial intercepts describe starting performance and are not entered as a separate treatment effect; random-effect variances are not treated as observed-score SDs.

not_extracted.what: Pilot study used to calibrate creativity and analytical-thinking rubrics
not_extracted.reason: The pilot used twelve students outside the main sample, with no randomized AI comparison or numerical treatment effect reported; it is also below the minimum participant count. PDF p. 7, Section 3.4; PDF p. 5, Section 3.1.

not_extracted.what: Analytical-thinking rubric scores, adjusted group contrast, and latent growth parameters
not_extracted.reason: The separate analytical tasks assess harmonic/structural labeling accuracy, theoretical justification, reasoning depth, and transfer. They measure music-analysis competence rather than creativity or quality of the creative musical products, and are not a convergent creativity test with scored correct answers. PDF p. 7, Section 3.3; Tables 3, 5, and 6; Figure 2.

The intercepts describe starting levels, not the effect of the current AI intervention on subsequent output. Baseline tasks are described as preceding intervention, although their exact relationship to Week 1 access remains unclear. PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; PDF pp. 8-9, Results RQ1 and Table 3.

not_extracted.what: Growth-model fit indices, random intercept/slope variances, and intercept-slope covariances
not_extracted.reason: These describe model fit and individual variation or baseline-growth associations, not a full-sample AI-versus-control treatment effect. The random-factor variances are not participant-level observed-score SDs and were not converted. PDF p. 6, Table 2; PDF pp. 8-9, Results RQ1.

not_extracted.what: Effects of prior ChatGPT use and baseline creativity/analytical covariates
not_extracted.reason: Covariate effects do not estimate the randomized current instructional-group contrast. The instructional Group / Creativity row is extracted separately. PDF p. 9, Results RQ2; PDF pp. 11-12, Tables 4-5.

This omnibus test combines the eligible creativity score with the separate analytical competence outcome and does not isolate a creativity outcome. The creativity-specific univariate effect and adjusted means are retained. PDF p. 11, Table 4; PDF p. 9, Results RQ2.

not_extracted.what: Cross-lagged/autoregressive paths and endpoint creativity-analytical correlations
not_extracted.reason: These estimate associations between performances and compare those associations across groups, including adjustment for earlier post-assignment outcomes; they are not full-sample effects of AI on the creativity level of output. PDF pp. 9-10, Results RQ3; PDF p. 12, Table 7.

not_extracted.what: Epistemic network co-occurrences and weekly activation of creative idea, creative revision, analytical check, and analytical structure
not_extracted.reason: These are process analyses of the experimental group only, with no AI-versus-comparison-arm contrast. Move activation is not an output fluency or across-person diversity effect. PDF p. 10, Results RQ4; PDF pp. 13-14, Figures 3-4 and Table 8.

not_extracted.what: Markov transition probabilities between creative and analytical moves
not_extracted.reason: Transitions are derived from the experimental group only and describe interaction processes, with no randomized between-arm output contrast. PDF pp. 10-12, Results RQ5; PDF pp. 15-16, Figures 5-6.

not_extracted.what: Occasion-specific creativity means and endpoint values shown only as plotted growth trajectories
not_extracted.reason: Figure 1 supplies no numeric data labels for individual points. Reading values from the axes would require estimation, which is prohibited. The tabled latent growth slopes are retained instead. PDF p. 10, Figure 1; PDF p. 9, Table 3.

open_items: The number of randomized classes per arm and allocation implementation are unreported (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1). The current codebook requires at least two classes per arm; the reconciled form's older assertion that no class-count minimum applies is superseded. Extraction retains the explicit class-randomization report without assuming that the minimum is met.

Class-adjusted uncertainty is not reported for either retained analysis. The student-level precision must not be treated as precision based on independent randomized classes (PDF pp. 8-9, Sections 3.7 and 4; PDF p. 12, Tables 5-6).

Participant-level observed creativity-score SDs by arm are absent. Table 6 contains adjusted-mean SEs, while growth-model random-effect variances are different quantities. No SD or standardized mean difference was derived.
The measurement occasion or aggregation defining the adjusted MANCOVA dependent variable is not stated (PDF p. 9, Results RQ2; PDF p. 12, Table 6).

It is unclear whether the Week 1 covariates were measured before any current ChatGPT access. The paper calls them baseline scores and describes pre-intervention baseline tasks, but supported tasks start in the opening weeks (PDF pp. 5-6 and 9). If these covariates are post-treatment, the adjusted contrast would fail the extraction rule for post-treatment adjustment.

Calendar weeks and measurement occasions are inconsistently described: weekly assessments, biweekly submissions across twenty-four weeks, and figures/analyses labeled across twelve weeks. The latent slope time unit therefore cannot be confirmed (PDF pp. 5, 7-10).

The growth model does not print analysis-specific participant counts or a between-arm slope-difference test, difference SE, or interval. The arm-parameter p-value bounds are printed as < .000 and cannot be repaired from the paper (PDF p. 9, Table 3).

How the rubric dimensions and the two external ratings were combined is unspecified, and output-score inter-rater reliability is not reported. Interaction-log coding reliability measures a different construct (PDF pp. 6-7, Sections 3.3 and 3.5).
Whether participants retained their condition from Zhou and Kim’s earlier study and how earlier exposure maps to present class allocation are not reported (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1).

The baseline-comparability claim cites tables that contain instructional descriptions and growth-model fit rather than baseline balance tests; the actual balance statistics are unavailable (PDF pp. 5-6).

Data are available on request, and no appendix, supplement, or public dataset is identified in the PDF. Missing counts, class identifiers, model definitions, and SDs cannot be resolved from the on-file source (PDF p. 17, Data availability).
notes: Extracted independently as B on 2026-10-10 from the on-file journal PDF. Read all 98,175 characters of the markdown conversion in consecutive chunks, including end matter and references. Inspected every table and figure before completing methods review; all quoted numeric values were verified using pymupdf text on the cited page, with text-strategy table recovery for key rows. PDF page indices plus one agree with printed page numbers. No appendix appears in the PDF and no c148 supplement is listed in the local supplement manifest. The statistical inventory comprised growth-model fit, initial levels and growth rates, random-factor variances/covariances, MANCOVA/univariate group and covariate tests, adjusted arm levels, cross-lagged associations, and experimental-arm process analyses. Only the adjusted creativity-score comparison and the creativity growth-slope comparison answer the in-scope current-assistance question; exclusions are itemized. No separate contrasts for the individual creativity-rubric dimensions are printed. The paper calls the design quasi-experimental but explicitly reports random class assignment. Class count and precision limitations are retained, rather than inferring individual randomization. All scored intervention products were made with AI available to the experimental group. The follow-up title does not denote a withdrawal test: whether effects persist after AI is removed is proposed as future research (PDF p. 16, Section 5.3). There is no across-people diversity outcome. No effects, SDs, uncertainty measures, graph values, or missing sample counts have been computed or guessed.
